title: VM Datastore Read and Write IOPS Threshold
exclusions: Returns VM/datastore/instance series whose 15-minute average read requests per second plus average write requests per second exceeds a local 500-IOPS review threshold, only when both series are present. Broadcom defines `datastore.numberReadAveraged` and `datastore.numberWriteAveraged` as rates in commands per second; Splunk indexes them as `vmware.vm.datastore.numberReadAveraged` and `vmware.vm.datastore.numberWriteAveraged` with unit `number`. The value is I/O operations per second, not interval request count, bytes/s, latency, queue depth, throughput, SIOC activity, a datastore limit, throttling, contention, or application impact. The 500 threshold is an example requiring workload/datastore baselining, not VMware guidance. Missing metrics are health failures. The rule changes no storage or VM setting.
evidence: After deployment, retain VM/datastore/host topology and owners; add-on allowlist, vCenter statistic level and collection interval; representative metric points with names, values, unit, aggregation and dimensions; vSphere performance-chart and storage-array/application comparisons; dual-series/DCN/index health; threshold/baseline approval; version-controlled `vsphere_vm_datastore_iops_threshold` SPL, ACL, schedule, dispatches and rows; dashboard/runbook and disposition; and dated read-only, write-only, both, boundary, missing-series, duplicate, delayed, vMotion, Storage vMotion and instance tests. This documentation review generated no I/O load, vCenter metric, search execution, storage diagnosis, alert, remediation or production validation evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated metrics bucket for one VM UUID and datastore/instance, supply complete read and write rate series with `unit=number`. Use a 15-minute mean of 350 read requests/s and 200 write requests/s; expect exactly one row with `read_iops=350`, `write_iops=200`, `total_iops=550`, threshold 500 and UC-2.1.17.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero rows when complete read plus write equals exactly 500 or less. Do not return a detection when either metric is absent, dimensions or unit are blank/wrong, the metric/index is wrong, or data is outside the closed range or exact replay. Separate health must expose incomplete pairs, duplicate routes, stale topology and collection delay.

dataSources: Primary source is vCenter VM datastore performance collected by Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics into the deployment-selected metrics index (example/default `index=vmware-perf-metrics`). Allowlist `datastore.average.numberReadAveraged.number` and `datastore.average.numberWriteAveraged.number`, indexed as `vmware.vm.datastore.numberReadAveraged` and `vmware.vm.datastore.numberWriteAveraged`. Both are rate metrics representing average read/write requests per second. Required dimensions are VM `uuid`/`name`, datastore, per-device `instance`, vCenter, hypervisor, unit/aggregation and metric time. Datastore latency, array telemetry, VM application SLOs, topology and Storage I/O Control status are corroborating sources.
app: Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics (Splunkbase 5089) collects VM/datastore metrics through vCenter and DCNs. A local storage-observability app owns allowlists, threshold/baseline policy, completeness health, saved search, topology enrichment, dashboard, tests, routing and runbook.
spl:
| mstats avg(vmware.vm.datastore.numberReadAveraged) AS read_iops avg(vmware.vm.datastore.numberWriteAveraged) AS write_iops WHERE index=vmware-perf-metrics earliest=-30m@m latest=-15m@m BY uuid name datastore instance vcenter hypervisor_name
| where len(uuid)>0 AND len(name)>0 AND len(datastore)>0 AND len(instance)>0 AND isnotnull(read_iops) AND isnotnull(write_iops)
| eval total_iops=read_iops+write_iops, threshold_iops=500
| where total_iops>threshold_iops
| eval read_iops=round(read_iops,2), write_iops=round(write_iops,2), total_iops=round(total_iops,2), window_seconds=900, use_case="UC-2.1.17"
| table uuid name datastore instance vcenter hypervisor_name read_iops write_iops total_iops threshold_iops window_seconds use_case
| sort 0 -total_iops name datastore instance
description: Identifies each VM/datastore device series whose complete read and write request-rate telemetry averages more than a locally selected 500 total IOPS across one closed 15-minute window. Results preserve the directional IOPS values and review threshold.
value: A correctly unit-labeled high-IOPS queue helps storage and workload teams find demand concentration before shared-datastore symptoms spread. Separating workload rate from latency and throttling prevents high but healthy I/O from being misdiagnosed as a storage fault.
implementation: Allowlist the two VM datastore request-rate metrics, prove requests-per-second semantics and per-device dimensions, and schedule the delayed 15-minute search. Tune the local threshold by VM/datastore class, keep dual-series health, and correlate each row with latency, queueing, array and application evidence before action.
visualization: Use a table with VM UUID/name, datastore, device instance, host, read/write/total IOPS, 15-minute window, threshold/baseline, latency, array health, owner and disposition. Add directional trends and top consumers plus separate missing-series/DCN/topology panels. Label units `operations per second`; do not label a threshold row `throttled`.
schema: Splunk metrics-index series for vSphere VM datastore average request-rate counters
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. The VMware rate metrics, VM UUID, datastore/device dimensions and dual-series completeness are metrics-index contracts, not published CIM Performance fields. Use `mstats`.

knownFalsePositives:
High IOPS is often legitimate demand, so every row is a review signal.

1. **Backup, replication or snapshot consolidation** — scheduled jobs can drive expected I/O. Match VM, datastore, job and exact interval; inspect latency and missed SLA.

2. **Database maintenance or batch processing** — index rebuilds, ETL, close and analytics can exceed static thresholds. Compare application calendar and owner-approved baseline.

3. **Patch or deployment activity** — package installation and image updates can create short high-I/O windows. Correlate lifecycle events and recurrence.

4. **Storage vMotion or migration** — topology and datastore dimensions can change while substantial I/O occurs. Reconcile migration events and source/destination series.

5. **Healthy high-performance tier** — 500 IOPS may be trivial on one datastore and material on another. Tune by service class, latency and capacity; the default is not vendor guidance.

6. **Metric duplication or aggregation drift** — duplicate collectors, changed intervals or dimensions can inflate/reshape averages. Validate one series and native rate semantics.

7. **Device-instance ambiguity** — aggregate and per-device series can overlap. Inventory instance and collection level; do not sum duplicate scopes.

8. **Workload relocation/rename** — names and hosts change. Use VM UUID and event-time datastore/topology for ownership.

**Suppression mechanism:** use an effective-dated post-result lookup keyed by vCenter, VM UUID, datastore/instance, workload schedule and threshold policy, with owner, evidence and finite expiry. Retain raw metrics and completeness/latency health; never suppress all high IOPS on a datastore.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and units

Assign vSphere, storage, application and Splunk owners. Inventory VM UUIDs, virtual disks/device instances, datastores, ESXi hosts, storage tiers, owners, workload calendars and SLOs. Broadcom documents numberReadAveraged and numberWriteAveraged as average commands issued per second during the collection interval. They are rate metrics with unit `number` and average rollup. The supplied 500 total IOPS threshold is local and must be tuned.

## Step 1 — Collect the optional metrics

Deploy supported Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics with vCenter API access over TCP 443 and `hostvmperf` enabled. Add `datastore.average.numberReadAveraged.number` and `datastore.average.numberWriteAveraged.number` to the VM metric allowlist. Confirm output in the actual metrics index under `vmware.vm.datastore.numberReadAveraged` and `vmware.vm.datastore.numberWriteAveraged`.

Compare selected VM/datastore/device series with vSphere Client performance charts over the same interval. Prove `_value`, unit, aggregation, UUID/name, datastore, instance, vCenter, hypervisor and `_time`. Build separate health for both names per expected series, interval, duplicates, collection level, DCN jobs, delay, topology freshness and missing dimensions. Never turn absent write/read telemetry into zero.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the search

Save sidecar SPL as `vsphere_vm_datastore_iops_threshold` and run every 15 minutes. At 12:30 the query covers 12:00–12:15. Move both bounds together after measuring p99 collection delay; reconcile late points separately.

`mstats avg` preserves the source rate meaning across the search window. The query groups by VM UUID, datastore and instance, requires both directional results, adds read and write rates, then applies strict `>500`; exactly 500 does not return. Values are rounded only after comparison. Do not use `sum` on these rate series to claim request count, and do not call the result throttling.

## Step 3 — Validate and tune

Test read-only, write-only, both, exact 500, above/below, absent direction, wrong unit, aggregate/per-device overlap, duplicate point/route, vMotion, Storage vMotion, rename, delayed/future time and wrong index. Compare known workload intervals with vSphere Client and array/application telemetry.

Develop thresholds by datastore class and workload baseline using owner-approved history. Pair IOPS with total read/write latency in milliseconds, queue depth where available, array/fabric health and application latency. High IOPS with low latency can be healthy; low IOPS with high latency can be critical. If monitoring SIOC, collect and validate its specific activity/latency fields rather than inferring throttling from IOPS.

## Step 4 — Operationalize and respond

Dashboard rate, directional split, datastore/tier, latency, baseline, owner and source health. Triage: verify metric/unit/series; inspect topology changes and scheduled workloads; compare datastore/host/array contention and latency; check guest/application SLOs; identify noisy-neighbor impact; then propose a reviewed action.

Never automatically alter SIOC shares, VM disk limits, storage policy, queue depth, multipathing, placement or workload schedule. Storage changes can create data and availability risk. Require storage/application approval, compatibility checks, rollback and before/after evidence.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot

- No IOPS metrics: verify allowlist, vCenter statistic level, `hostvmperf`, index, API/DCN health and RBAC.
- One direction absent: fail completeness health; do not fill null with zero.
- Values disagree with vSphere: align entity/device, range, interval, rollup, unit and timezone.
- Values are inflated: inspect duplicate collectors, aggregate plus per-device overlap and use of sum versus average.
- Datastore/instance blank: verify per-device collection and dimensions before alerting.
- High IOPS without latency: classify as demand, not fault, until impact evidence exists.
- Suspected throttling: collect native SIOC/limit and latency evidence; this rule alone cannot prove it.

Keep status draft until VMware, storage and Splunk owners validate collection, thresholds, fixtures and response. Documentation review is not production benchmarking.
grandmaExplanation: We show virtual machines that are making more storage requests per second than a locally chosen review level. A busy machine is not automatically unhealthy or being slowed down, so the team also checks delay, storage capacity and the application's normal schedule.
